extracted.intended_audience: literate early-18th-century London readers; subscribers of The Spectator; general readers interested in theatre, poetry, manners and public affairs
extracted.subtask_description: Short essays and letters offering criticism and prescriptive remarks on theatre, music, poetry (Milton), travel as part of education, and public regulation (food/drink vendors). The page gives evaluative principles for artistic quality, pedagogy, public health regulation, and social decorum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate use of the Cat-call in British theatre
rubrics_metrics.description: The Cat-call exerts itself to most advantage in the British Theatre: It very much Improves the Sound of Nonsense, and often goes along with the Voice of the Actor, as the Violin or Harpsichord accompanies the Italian Recitativo.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the Cat-call as a stage instrument to heighten comic or nonsensical passages, as a substitute for an ancient chorus, and to accompany or comment upon actors' voices. Skilled practitioners have base and treble cat-calls (former for Tragedy, latter for Comedy), specialized squeaks to denote violations of dramatic unities, and varied notes (smut-note, fustian-note, stupid-note) to indicate the target (poet or player) or the fault.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match musical instrument to intended emotional effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Musical instruments should be suited to the effect sought — Collier speculates about inventing an 'Anti-Musick' that 'shall sink the Spirits, and shake the Nerves, and curdle the Blood, and inspire Despair, and Cowardice and Consternation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select or invent instruments whose timbre and imitation (e.g., roars, howls, cat-warbles) produce the desired emotional response; consider appropriateness of such effects to context (theatre vs. military/camp).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider audience reaction as part of theatrical critique
rubrics_metrics.description: Audience devices (like the Cat-call) can materially affect performers and the reception of a piece — the Cat-call has 'struck a Damp into Generals, and frighted Heroes off the Stage.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for how public noises and audience interventions influence the dignity, success, or failure of a performance; critics and practitioners should note when audience instruments change the perceived merit of actors or plays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inspect and regulate vendors to protect public health
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who vend Wines should be under oaths; an officer should inspect itinerant provision-dealers and enquiry where they buy their wares.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public officials should regularly inspect signs and sellers, verify sources of food/drink, and make public representations about those who preserve or endanger public health (praising honest importers and censuring adulterators).

rubrics_metrics.name: Severe legal liability for adulterating food/drink that causes death
rubrics_metrics.description: If a vintner mixes wine so that the drinker dies within a Year and a Day after taking it, he should be deemed guilty of wilful Murder and punished accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposed legal framework: oath-bound vendors; Quarter Sessions to inform the county; jury instructed to inquire and present delinquents; no mitigation by chance or manslaughter if malice/willing false mixture is proved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Travel should be the final stage of a young man's education
rubrics_metrics.description: Travel is really the last Step to be taken in the Institution of Youth; to set out with it is to begin where they should end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not send very young men abroad before they have fixed in their minds first principles of manners, behaviour and language; travel without foundational education results in gawdy, superficial impressions rather than real benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purposes of travel: study customs, policies, and improve taste by seeing originals
rubrics_metrics.description: The true End of visiting Foreign Parts is to look into their Customs and Policies, unlearn odd Peculiarities in our Manners, and improve our Taste of the best Authors of Antiquity by seeing the Places where they lived.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use travel to compare foreign and native institutions, to temper affectations learned at home, to examine celebrated localities that illustrate classical authors, and to draw moral lessons from ruins and historical sites; travel is pedagogically valuable when the traveller is prepared to make these observations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose competent tutors for travel; avoid mere cheap companionship
rubrics_metrics.description: It is common to send lads abroad 'under the Tuition of some poor Scholar, who is willing to be banished for thirty Pounds a Year,' leading to little advantage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the travelling companion/tutor is skilled and able to direct the traveller's learning; avoid cheap, incompetent escorts that leave the young man to gawk rather than to study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Musical selection should fit ceremonial occasion
rubrics_metrics.description: Warlike Sounds (drums) are very improper in a Marriage-Consort and give great Offence; they insinuate that the Joys of this State are short.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select soft airs for matrimonial or similarly delicate ceremonies; avoid martial music that suggests discord or ill-omen for celebrations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy should be tempered with moral severity for reasonable audiences
rubrics_metrics.description: Mirth ought to be seasoned with a certain Severity, which ought to recommend it to People who pretend to keep Reason and Authority over all their Actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Playwrights and performers should balance humour with moral seriousness so that entertainments are enjoyable without encouraging vice; this makes comedy acceptable to more moral-minded spectators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variety and progressive development of passions in narrative poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Milton shows a wonderful Art in describing variety of Passions which arise in our first Parents upon the Breach: passing from Triumph of Guilt through Remorse, Shame, Despair, Contrition, Prayer, and Hope, to a perfect and compleat Repentance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct moral/emotional arcs so passions develop logically and culminate in a convincing resolution (e.g., repentance); sequence emotions to show internal change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suit parts of a poem to the characters/actors introduced
rubrics_metrics.description: The Author never fails to give a poetical Turn to his Sentiments; he always suits his Parts to the Actors whom he introduces (e.g., Michael is employed suitably in the Expulsion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match diction, action, and rhetorical register to the rank and role of the characters; grand personages warrant more solemn, martial, or elevated portrayals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrate scriptural/poetical passages with poetical imagination
rubrics_metrics.description: Milton has finely wrought scriptural passages into his narration (e.g., the incense and prayers allegory) giving them a poetical turn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When drawing on sacred or traditional material, transform rather than merely quote it — impart a poetical twist that serves the narrative and elevates imagery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use striking prodigies and imagery that suit the fable and effect
rubrics_metrics.description: The description of the Sun in an Eclipse, the descending bright cloud with an Host of Angels, and the whole Theatre of Nature darkened to make the glorious Machine appear, are examples of imagery that support the fable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ prodigies or supernatural images sparingly and in ways that heighten the central action and moral meaning rather than distract; ensure imagery is congruent with the story's stakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ contrast and opposition to enrich poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: There is nothing more delightful in Poetry than a Contrast and Opposition of Incidents (e.g., moving from melancholy prospects of death to a Scene of Mirth, Love, and Jollity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use juxtaposition of moods and scenes to create variety and emphasize themes; alternate sorrow and joy to heighten emotional effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid puerile or redundant imagery; prefer dignity and aptness
rubrics_metrics.description: Milton avoids the puerile or redundant images found in Ovid (e.g., 'Wolf swimming among the Sheep'), choosing instead more solemn and just descriptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refrain from idle or frivolous conceits on grave occasions; choose images that sustain the poem's dignity and do not incur critical censure for triviality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comprehensive plan and completeness of action in epic poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Milton's plan is in many particulars greater than that of the Iliad or Æneid; had he not represented expulsion from Paradise, his Fall of Man would not have been compleat, and consequently his Action imperfect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the epic's action is rounded and complete; include necessary episodes (even if smaller) that render the central theme and moral fully intelligible and concluded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gender-appropriate tone in character speeches
rubrics_metrics.description: Eve's Complaint is 'particularly soft and womanish'; Adam's Speech is 'more masculine and elevated.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor the tone, diction, and emotional expression of speeches to the character's gender, station, and temperament as understood by the intended audience, to achieve plausibility and aesthetic fit.
